text: Danh Võ, born Võ Trung Kỳ Danh on August 5, 1975, is a contemporary artist of Vietnamese descent who lives and works in Berlin and Mexico City. He was born in Vũng Tàu, Vietnam, and after the fall of Saigon in 1975, his family, along with 20,000 other South Vietnamese, was relocated to the island of Phú Quốc. In 1979, when he was four years old, his family fled Vietnam in a homemade boat and was rescued by a Danish Maersk freighter, eventually settling in Denmark. Their assimilation into European culture and the circumstances of their escape are central themes in Võ’s art, which blends historical and personal elements. When registered by Danish authorities, the family name Võ was listed last, and his middle name, Trung Kỳ, was recorded as his first name. Võ moved to Berlin in 2005 after completing his education at Städelschule in Frankfurt, having previously left the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts in Copenhagen. He has held residencies at Villa Aurora in Los Angeles (2006), Kadist Art Foundation in Paris (2009), and Villa Medici in Rome (2013). His installations often feature documents, photos, and appropriated works, exploring identity and belonging. The conceptual work Vo Rosasco Rasmussen (2002–) documents his marriages and divorces from significant figures in his life, with each spouse’s last name retained; his current official name is Trung Kỳ Danh Võ Rosasco Rasmussen. Oma Totem (2009) displays his grandmother’s welcome gifts from a German relief program in the 1980s, including a television set, washing machine, and refrigerator adorned with her crucifix. For 2.02.1861 (2009–), Võ asked his father Phung Võ to transcribe the last letter from French Catholic Saint Théophane Vénard to his father before his 1861 execution in Vietnam; although 1,200 copies exist as of 2017, the total number remains undefined until Phung Võ’s death. In Autoerotic Asphyxiation (2010), Võ presents photographs of young Asian men taken by Joseph Carrier, an American anthropologist who worked in Vietnam for the RAND Corporation from 1962 to 1973 and later bequeathed his archive to Võ. For We the People (2010–2012), Võ commissioned a Shanghai fabricator to recast a life-size Statue of Liberty from 30 tons of copper sheets just two pennies wide; instead of assembling the approximately 300 sections, the elements were shipped to about 15 global sites after production in China. The work was installed in New York City from mid-May to early December 2014 under the Public Art Fund, with parts displayed in City Hall Park and Brooklyn Bridge Park, though some chain link replicas were stolen during installation. Today, parts of We the People (2011–2013) remain in museum collections, including the Pérez Art Museum Miami, and was named No.5 of "The 25 Best Works of the 21st Century" by Frieze. In 2013, for a show at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, Võ created a homage to Martin Wong, consisting of nearly 4,000 small artworks and artifacts from Wong’s life, displayed in a gallery lined with laminated plywood shelves, with the title "I am you and you are too" appearing on Wong’s business cards and stamps. A 2013 exhibition at Marian Goodman Gallery featured personal items from U.S. Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara, including the pen used to sign the Gulf of Tonkin memo and a 1944 Ansel Adams photograph. In 2016, frustrated by rising Berlin rents, Võ and artists Rirkrit Tiravanija, Nairy Baghramian, and Haegue Yang found the 5,000 m² Güldenhof in Stechlin, Brandenburg—a former pig farm with 18th-century stone barns—transforming it into his studio from 2017 to 2020. Võ won the 2012 Hugo Boss Prize, the BlauOrange Kunstpreis in 2007, and was a nominee for the Preis der Nationalgalerie für junge Kunst in 2009. His first solo exhibition was in 2005 at Galerie Klosterfelde in Berlin. He participated in the Venice Biennale in 2013 and has exhibited at the Walker Art Center, Art Institute of Chicago, Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, Musée d'art moderne de la Ville de Paris, Kunsthaus Bregenz, and Kunsthalle Mainz. In 2014, he shared an exhibition with Carol Rama at Nottingham Contemporary and opened "الحجارة وادي" (Wād al-ḥaŷara) at Museo Jumex in Mexico City on November 14. From February 9 to May 9, 2018, the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum presented Danh Vo: Take My Breath Away, the first comprehensive U.S. survey of his work. M+ partnered with the Isamu Noguchi Foundation and Garden Museum for the exhibition Noguchi for Danh Vo: Counterpoint (November 16, 2018 – April 22, 2019) in Hong Kong’s M+ Pavilion. Recent exhibitions include CAPC, Bordeaux (2018); National Museum of Art Osaka (2020); Secession, Vienna (2021); Mudam Luxembourg (2021); Bourse de Commerce, Paris (2023); and Xavier Hufkens (2023). In 2014, Dutch collector Bert Kreuk sued Võ, claiming an agreement to create new works for his exhibition Transforming the Known at the Gemeentemuseum Den Haag, which would be acquired by Kreuk. Before the exhibition, Võ sent an existing work, Fiat Veritas (2013), a gold-leafed cardboard box. Kreuk argued for a new large-scale work from Võ’s Budweiser or American Flag series. In June 2015, a Rotterdam court upheld the claim and ordered Võ to create new work within a year. In July 2015, Võ proposed a site-specific wall piece with the text "Shove it up your ass, you faggot," which led to a settlement and the dismissal of the suit. Võ currently lives in Berlin and Brandenburg and renovated a century-old home in Mexico City’s Roma Norte neighborhood. He is in a relationship with photographer Heinz Peter Knes.
